title: Perf metric pipeline validation notes (TTFT/TPOT ground-truth audit)
content:
Context / why this doc exists
- We’re about to lock Q1’26 performance baselines (TTFT, TPOT, throughput). Before we treat these as release gates, we need high confidence that:
  (a) runtime-emitted telemetry matches “ground truth” wall-clock timings from the client side, and
  (b) the metrics pipeline (ingestion -> aggregation -> dashboard) preserves the definitions.
- This is specifically about correctness, not “making numbers look good”.

Owners / on-call escalation
- Primary: Nadia Rahman (token-level metrics correctness)
- Pipeline: Logan Wright / Caleb Johnson
- Consumers: perf suite / baseline gating: Marcus Reed; SRE variance: Sean Gallagher

Definitions (as used in baseline docs)
- TTFT (time-to-first-token)
  - Non-streaming: time from request accepted by server to the time the first generated token is available (internally) and/or first byte sent (externally). In practice our dashboards have been using server timestamps; this validation checks the delta to client-observed “first chunk arrival”.
  - Streaming: time from request accepted by server to first streamed chunk sent (not “first chunk fully received”). See “known gaps” for edge cases.
- TPOT (time-per-output-token)
  - Effective decode rate: (time from first token to end-of-generation) / (number of output tokens after first token). We also track instantaneous decode timing internally, but baseline uses the effective measure.

What we validated
1) Runtime timing stamps correctness
- Server-side events we rely on:
  - request_received_ts
  - prefill_start_ts
  - prefill_end_ts
  - first_token_ready_ts (internal)
  - first_chunk_sent_ts (streaming)
  - generation_end_ts
  - output_token_count
- Primary metric computations:
  - TTFT_server_internal = first_token_ready_ts - request_received_ts
  - TTFT_server_streaming = first_chunk_sent_ts - request_received_ts
  - TPOT_server_effective = (generation_end_ts - first_token_ready_ts) / (output_token_count - 1)

2) Client “ground truth” measurement
- We built a small harness that measures:
  - t0_client: right before HTTP request write
  - t_headers: when response headers available
  - t_first_chunk: when first streaming chunk is received (client clock)
  - t_end: when stream completes (client clock)
- Harness stores:
  - request_id (from response header)
  - model, region, deployment mode
  - prompt token count (client-side tokenizer)
  - output token count (parsed)
  - network metadata (client region, ISP type when available)

3) Pipeline integrity
- Verified the metric names/units at each hop:
  - runtime -> collector -> aggregation -> grafana queries
- Confirmed we’re not accidentally mixing milliseconds/microseconds in derived calculations (this has bitten us before).

Sampling strategy
Goal: enough coverage to catch systemic issues, without exploding cost/cardinality.
- Period: 2026-01-20 through 2026-02-14 (includes initial baseline runner bring-up + a few runtime patches)
- Environments:
  - Hosted API (primary)
  - Dedicated pool (1 tenant used for internal testing)
- Regions sampled:
  - us-east
  - us-west
  - eu-central
- Models sampled (baseline-critical):
  - 7B chat (short-context high QPS)
  - 13B chat (mixed)
  - long-context variant (stress streaming TTFT + long prefill)
- Traffic shapes:
  - non-streaming, short prompt (p50 ~200 tok)
  - streaming, short prompt
  - streaming, long prompt (p50 ~6k tok)
  - bursty concurrency ramp (1 -> 32 concurrent)
- Selection:
  - For each (region, model, traffic shape):
    - 30 runs x 3 trials/run (90 data points)
    - mix of warm and cold cache (see below)
- Cache conditions:
  - cold: restart runner pod, ensure KV/prefix cache disabled OR randomized prefix
  - warm: 5-minute warmup using same distribution, then sample 30 “steady state” requests

How comparisons were done
- For each sampled request:
  - join client measurements to server telemetry by request_id
  - compute deltas:
    - delta_TTFT = TTFT_client_first_chunk - TTFT_server_streaming (for streaming)
    - delta_TTFT_internal = TTFT_client_first_chunk - TTFT_server_internal (tracked but not used for streaming baseline)
    - delta_TPOT = TPOT_client_effective - TPOT_server_effective
- We report:
  - median / p95 of delta (absolute)
  - bias direction (server systematically lower/higher)
  - correlation (Pearson) between server and client measures
- Pass/fail rubric (for baseline gating readiness):
  - Streaming TTFT: median |delta| <= 25ms; p95 |delta| <= 75ms (NOTE: this is strict; see network caveat)
  - Non-streaming TTFT (client vs server internal): median |delta| <= 40ms; p95 |delta| <= 120ms
  - TPOT: median |delta| <= 2.5%; p95 |delta| <= 7.5%

Results summary (as of 2026-02-14)
- TPOT (effective) looks good.
  - Across all regions/models, TPOT_server_effective closely tracks client effective decode (high correlation).
  - Biggest errors show up when client parsing undercounts tokens (SSE chunk boundaries + whitespace). We fixed parsing in harness; server side was consistent.
- Non-streaming TTFT is generally OK, but client deltas include network + TLS + request queueing before request_received_ts.
  - delta median typically +15–30ms (client > server) as expected.
- Streaming TTFT had a real instrumentation issue.
  - Before fix: in some cases first_chunk_sent_ts was stamped after the chunk was actually written, inflating server TTFT (i.e., server reported worse TTFT than client sometimes, which is a red flag).
  - Root cause: first chunk callback firing after buffer flush. Fixed in redwood/pr-23944.
  - After fix: streaming TTFT deltas are stable and have the expected sign (client >= server) except for a small set of cases noted below.

Key findings (details)
1) Request_received timestamp definition mismatch with client t0
- request_received_ts is stamped after request has been accepted by the server handler (post some proxy layers).
- For baseline methodology this is fine because we’re measuring platform runtime performance, not client network.
- For customer-facing comparisons, we must be explicit that baseline TTFT uses server-side start.

2) Streaming TTFT edge case (FIXED)
- Symptom: server streaming TTFT p50 increased by ~40–80ms on some long-context streaming runs, but clients did not observe it.
- Root cause: incorrect timestamp for first chunk (first_chunk_sent_ts). It was taken after chunk assembly and buffer flush scheduling.
- Fix: PR-23944.
- Action: baseline suite should enforce runtime version >= PR-23944 for any “locked” baselines.

3) Token counting consistency
- output_token_count in telemetry is based on runtime tokenizer (server).
- client token counting is often based on SDK tokenizer or a model-specific tokenizer. These can diverge (especially around special tokens / tool-call formatting).
- For TPOT comparisons we now rely on server output_token_count for the denominator when comparing server-vs-client effective decode timing (otherwise you can manufacture a TPOT delta by using a different tokenizer).
- Known gap: customers will experience “their tokenizer”, so externally we need to state how tokens are counted.

4) Cache warmup annotation is incomplete in pipeline (KNOWN GAP)
- We can distinguish “cache enabled/disabled” by config, but we cannot reliably label “cache hit rate” per-request in aggregated TTFT/TPOT dashboards yet.
- This matters because TTFT can be very sensitive to prefix cache hits in some workloads.
- Recommendation: add per-request cache_state annotation (hit/miss/partial) and aggregate to a coarse dimension (avoid cardinality blowup). Runtime work likely overlaps with KV cache annotations (see upcoming runtime changes).

5) Clock skew isn’t the issue, but client/server comparison needs careful interpretation
- We are not trying to match absolute timestamps, only durations.
- Still, client durations include:
  - network transit time
  - client scheduling jitter
  - backpressure at proxies
- Therefore: “server TTFT < client TTFT” is expected. “server TTFT > client TTFT” should be rare and usually indicates instrumentation or join issues.

6) Metric pipeline: percentiles are correct, but one query mixes TTFT definitions (KNOWN GAP)
- Found one Grafana panel that used first_token_ready_ts for streaming TTFT, not first_chunk_sent_ts.
- This makes streaming TTFT look better than it should when chunking is delayed.
- Fix requested: update dashboard query + rename to make definition explicit.
- Owner: Sergio Costa (dashboards). (Logan to follow up.)

Open issues / known gaps
- (GAP-1) Per-request cache state label not yet in standard metric dimension set.
- (GAP-2) Streaming chunking policy changes can change “first chunk sent” without changing “first token ready”. For baseline purposes this is acceptable (it reflects real client-perceived responsiveness), but it complicates attribution to kernel vs scheduler.
- (GAP-3) Retry behavior in benchmark harness can bias tails if we silently retry slow requests. We need the runner to emit a “retried=true” flag and exclude or separately report.
- (GAP-4) Tokenization mismatches for tool calls / structured output: client-side output token counts can diverge significantly. For baseline, we should standardize on server token counts and treat client counts as informational only.

Recommended next steps (short)
1) Make PR-23944 a hard prerequisite for baseline runs and perf-canary.
2) Update dashboard panels to explicitly label TTFT definition (internal vs streaming-first-chunk).
3) Add cache_state annotation plan (coordinate with runtime KV cache counters work).
4) Bake this validation harness into ENG-4832 acceptance criteria:
   - run nightly on a small sample (cheap) to prevent regressions in telemetry.

Appendix A: Quick checklist when TTFT/TPOT looks “off”
- Is workload streaming or non-streaming? Which TTFT definition did the chart use?
- Does the runtime version include the streaming first-chunk timestamp fix?
- Are you comparing to client numbers that include network? (Don’t.)
- Did the workload run warm cache vs cold cache?
- Are token counts comparable (same tokenizer, same special token rules)?

Appendix B: Notes to self
- Once baseline artifacts are locked, we should pin the telemetry schema version too. Changes to field names/units can silently break dashboards.
- Consider adding a “telemetry sanity” gate to perf-canary: if server TTFT > client TTFT for >X% of requests, mark run invalid and page only if persistent.
